purpose: Quinine is used to treat malaria, a serious infection caused by a parasite spread through mosquito bites. It is specifically used for a type of malaria called uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria. In the past it was also used for leg cramps, but the FDA no longer recommends it for that purpose due to safety concerns.
how_it_works: Quinine works by interfering with the malaria parasite's ability to survive and grow inside your red blood cells. It essentially poisons the parasite by disrupting how it processes a substance it needs to live. This stops the parasite from multiplying and helps your body clear the infection.
common_side_effects: Very common side effects include ringing in your ears (tinnitus), headache, dizziness, blurred vision, nausea, vomiting, stomach upset, and flushing or sweating. These effects together are sometimes called 'cinchonism' and are well known with this medicine.
warnings: Quinine can cause a dangerous drop in blood sugar, especially in pregnant women. It can also cause serious heart rhythm problems, so tell your doctor if you have any heart conditions. A rare but serious reaction called blackwater fever or severe allergic reactions can occur. It can also lower your platelet count, increasing bleeding risk. Do not take quinine for leg cramps — the risks outweigh the benefits for that use. Tell your doctor about all your medications because quinine interacts with many drugs.
typical_dosing: The usual adult dose for malaria is 648 mg (two 324 mg capsules) taken by mouth three times a day for 7 days. It is almost always used together with a second antibiotic medicine. Always take it exactly as your doctor prescribes and finish the full course even if you feel better.
